title: Cyber Seeds - Human Authority for the Agentic Web
pitch: WebMCP with human-held, fail-closed authority: agents can inspect and request sensitive changes, but cannot approve, replay or transfer consent.

WebMCP with human-held, fail-closed authority: agents can inspect and request sensitive changes, but cannot approve, replay or transfer consent.

 Inspiration 

 The web is becoming agentic. Browser agents can now discover site capabilities, inspect information and request actions on behalf of people. 

 That creates a question that is bigger than a confirmation button: 

 When an agent can perform a consequential action, where is the authority boundary that proves a human actually chose it? 

 Cyber Seeds is built around the idea that capability is not authority. An agent may be able to understand a problem and request a change, but it must not be able to create, reuse or redirect a human decision. 

 This prototype applies that principle to a synthetic household digital-safety scenario. 

 What it does 

 Cyber Seeds exposes three structured WebMCP tools: 

 
 inspect_demo_household — read-only 
 get_approval_state — read-only 
 perform_sensitive_change — a controlled consequential action 
 

 The agent can inspect the synthetic household dashboard and identify that the primary account lacks multi-factor authentication. It can then request that sensitive change. 

 Cyber Seeds fails closed. The request becomes pending and execution is refused with human_approval_missing . 

 The core demonstration is that the agent cannot approve itself. An agent-derived attempt to activate the visible approval control is rejected as untrusted_ui_event , because interaction is not consent. 

 A genuine human must manually approve the exact pending request. Once that happens, authority is bound to the specific action, target and request identity. The agent may retry that one approved MFA request, once. 

 After the change succeeds, the approval is consumed immediately. It cannot be replayed, and it cannot be transferred to a different action such as a router security update. That action receives its own separate pending request and requires its own human decision. 

 How I built it 

 I built Cyber Seeds as a live browser prototype using WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, deployed publicly on Cloudflare Pages. 

 The project combines: 

 
 Structured WebMCP tool registration 
 A synthetic household security model 
 A human approval gate outside the agent tool surface 
 Exact request, action and target binding 
 An authority ledger that records refusal, approval, execution and consumption 
 Explicit fail-closed states for unsafe or incomplete requests 
 

 The live page is intentionally designed so a judge can see both sides of the boundary: what an agent is permitted to discover and request, and what remains exclusively under human control. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The difficult part was not giving an agent a tool. It was ensuring that every shortcut failed safely. 

 I had to account for situations where an agent might try to: 

 
 Trigger a visible approval control itself 
 Retry a completed action 
 Reuse a consumed approval 
 Apply an approval to a different target 
 Act on stale or mismatched request data 
 

 A conventional “Are you sure?” prompt is not enough for that problem. The system needs to prove that approval came from the human, that it applies only to the intended consequence, and that it cannot be reused. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The submitted prototype demonstrates an end-to-end authority lifecycle: 

 
 The agent discovers structured WebMCP capabilities. 
 It inspects the synthetic household state. 
 It identifies a sensitive MFA issue. 
 Its first action attempt fails closed without human approval. 
 Its self-approval attempt is rejected. 
 A human manually approves the exact request. 
 The approved action executes once. 
 The authority is consumed. 
 Replay produces no second consequence. 
 Cross-target reuse is refused. 
 

 The implementation passed 32 automated checks covering fail-closed execution, exact request binding, parameter binding, untrusted UI events, denial, single-use authority, replay protection, stale requests and cross-target refusal. 

 Most importantly, the prototype turns a security principle into visible, testable behaviour: 

 
 Agents can request authority. They cannot manufacture it. 
 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP makes agent interaction more structured, discoverable and useful than relying on screen scraping or guessed UI flows. 

 But discoverability must be paired with governance. 

 The key learning from this project is that agent safety should not depend on an agent promising to behave. The authority boundary must be enforced by the application itself, with explicit evidence of what was requested, what the human approved, what executed and what is no longer valid. 

 What's next for Cyber Seeds — Human Authority for the Agentic Web 

 This submitted build remains frozen for evaluation. 

 Beyond the challenge, Cyber Seeds will explore how this authority model can support real-world domestic cyber-resilience workflows: household security reviews, scam-response support, account recovery guidance and practitioner-led safeguarding systems. 

 The longer-term aim is to develop practical patterns for a future where people and agents work together—but humans retain meaningful control over consequential decisions.
